titolo: twitter Vulnerability Disclosure Program
descrizione: twitter public bug bounty program

scope: App mobile su Google Play / App Store
outOfScope: Attacchi DDoS / volumetrici
Social engineering su dipendenti
Test su ambienti di produzione con dati reali di utenti
Spam o invio massivo di contenuti
Vulnerabilità in browser di terze parti (es. Chrome bugs)
Rate limiting issues senza impatto reale
Self-XSS (richiede azione della vittima)
Vulnerabilità che richiedono accesso fisico al device
Clickjacking su pagine senza azioni sensibili
Best practice senza impatto dimostrabile
Username/email enumeration su form pubblici
CSRF su endpoint non state-changing
Vulnerabilità già note pubblicamente senza PoC aggiuntivo
Problemi di SPF/DKIM/DMARC
Mixed content warnings su pagine non autenticabili

testingTechniques.name: Ricognizione & Enumerazione
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

reportingSteps: 1. REGISTRAZIONE: Crea un account sul programma e metti il tuo handle di test in bio
2. RACCOLTA PROVE: Cattura screenshot/video di OGNI step della riproduzione con timestamp
3. MINIMIZZAZIONE: Crea un account demo e un account vittima (no dati reali)
4. REDAZIONE REPORT: Segui il template del programma, includi: Summary, Impact, Steps to Reproduce, PoC, Remediation
5. IMPATTO BUSINESS: Spiega sempre "What can an attacker do?" non solo "How does it work"
6. CVSS SCORE: Calcola il punteggio CVSS v3.1 con cvss calculator
7. SUBMIT: Carica su HackerOne/Bugcrowd/Intigriti e attendi triage (24-72h)
8. DUPLICATI: Se è un dup, è normale. Continua a cacciare!
9. RETEST: Dopo il fix, verifica che la patch funzioni davvero
10. DISCLOSURE: Aspetta il permesso del programma prima di blog/tweet
quickStartGuide: Step 1: Leggi TUTTO il policy del programma su twitter
Step 2: Configura Burp Suite con il proxy del tuo browser (FoxyProxy)
Step 3: Crea due account: attaccante e vittima su due browser diversi
Step 4: Mappa tutte le feature: signup, login, profilo, pagamenti, API
Step 5: Inizia con OWASP Top 10 e tools automatici (nuclei, sqlmap)
Step 6: Testa manualmente la business logic (sconti, ruoli, workflow)
Step 7: Documenta OGNI cosa interessante
Step 8: Scrivi un report chiaro con PoC riproducibile in 5 minuti
Step 9: Submeti e rispondi velocemente a domande del triage
Step 10: Studia i report pubblici (HackerOne Hacktivity) per imparare
tips: 💡 Leggi almeno 50 report risolti su HackerOne Hacktivity prima di iniziare
💡 Concentrati su UN programma per almeno 2 settimane
💡 Le business logic bug pagano DI PIÙ delle XSS
💡 I bug race condition sono sottovalutati ma pagati
💡 Usa Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) per trovare endpoint dimenticati
💡 Controlla sempre le API mobile vs web
💡 Non riportare MAI self-XSS, clickjacking senza impatto
💡 Impara Burp a livello avanzato: macro, match/replace, scanner
💡 La qualità del report > quantità
💡 Network: Discord Bugcrowd, NahamSec, InsiderPhD, STÖK

testingTechniques.name: Ricognizione & Enumerazione
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

testingTechniques.name: API Endpoint Discovery
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutti gli endpoint API, parametri e metodi accettati
steps: Intercetta traffico con Burp Suite o OWASP ZAP
Usa kiterunner o wordlists API comuni
Testa metodi HTTP alternativi: PUT, DELETE, PATCH, OPTIONS
Verifica GraphQL introspection se presente
Leggi documentazione API pubblica su /docs, /swagger

testingTechniques.name: Mass Assignment
testingTechniques.description: Inietta campi non previsti nel body della richiesta
steps: Intercetta una richiesta PUT/POST normale
Aggiungi campi come: isAdmin true, role admin, verified true
Verifica se vengono accettati e modificano il tuo account
Testa con campi PII: ssn, creditCard, password
Prova con campi interni: internal_id, user_type

testingTechniques.name: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA)
testingTechniques.description: Accedi a oggetti di altri utenti cambiando ID
steps: Crea due account su due browser diversi
Cattura tutte le richieste con oggetti (es. /api/orders/123)
Sostituisci l'ID con uno dell'altro account
Se ottieni risposta 200 con dati altrui = BOLA confermato
Documenta sempre con screenshot prima/dopo

testingTechniques.name: Rate Limiting Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Bypassa limiti di velocità per brute force o scraping
steps: Identifica endpoint con rate limit (login, OTP, search)
Prova header X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, X-Originating-IP
Cambia case del path: /API/Login vs /api/login
Aggiungi parametri irrilevanti: ?a=1&a=2
Usa IP rotation con proxy/VPN

testingTechniques.name: GraphQL Specific
testingTechniques.description: Testa vulnerabilità specifiche di GraphQL
steps: Abilita introspection con query: {__schema{types{name}}}
Usa batch query per rate limit bypass
Cerca field deprecated o hidden
Testa nested query DoS con depth limiting
Verifica authorization a livello di field, non solo oggetto

titolo: CVE-2026-109973: The Image Hover Effects Ultimate Visual Composer (Flipbox - Awesomes Flip Boxes Image Overlay) plugi...
descrizione: The Image Hover Effects Ultimate Visual Composer (Flipbox - Awesomes Flip Boxes Image Overlay) plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'flip-box-image-upload-url-01-alt' parameter in versions up to, and including, 3.1.1. This is due to the plugin saving the image-alt field through sanitize_text_field() in Inc/Style22::register_child() (and Inc/Style18, 19, 20, 25, 29) — which preserves the double-quote character — and then concatenating the stored value into a double-quoted HTML attribute in Public_Render/Style22::default_render() (and the corresponding Style18/19/20/25/29 renderers) with no esc_attr() escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with contributor-level access and above (when an administrator has delegated the plugin's 'Who can edit' capability via the plugin Settings page, or on multisite installations where even administrators lack unfiltered_html), to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses any page containing an affected [oxilab_flip_box] shortcode or block.

steps: Identifica tutte le superfici di input/output
Mappa flusso dati end-to-end
Testa ogni input con fuzzing (boofuzz, radamsa)
Verifica configurazioni di default e credenziali
Documenta ogni anomalia con PoC riproducibile

reportingSteps: 1. REGISTRAZIONE: Crea un account sul programma e metti il tuo handle di test in bio
2. RACCOLTA PROVE: Cattura screenshot/video di OGNI step della riproduzione con timestamp
3. MINIMIZZAZIONE: Crea un account demo e un account vittima (no dati reali)
4. REDAZIONE REPORT: Segui il template del programma, includi: Summary, Impact, Steps to Reproduce, PoC, Remediation
5. IMPATTO BUSINESS: Spiega sempre "What can an attacker do?" non solo "How does it work"
6. CVSS SCORE: Calcola il punteggio CVSS v3.1 con cvss calculator
7. SUBMIT: Carica su HackerOne/Bugcrowd/Intigriti e attendi triage (24-72h)
8. DUPLICATI: Se è un dup, è normale. Continua a cacciare!
9. RETEST: Dopo il fix, verifica che la patch funzioni davvero
10. DISCLOSURE: Aspetta il permesso del programma prima di blog/tweet
quickStartGuide: Step 1: Leggi TUTTO il policy del programma su CVE-2026-120579
Step 2: Configura Burp Suite con il proxy del tuo browser (FoxyProxy)
Step 3: Crea due account: attaccante e vittima su due browser diversi
Step 4: Mappa tutte le feature: signup, login, profilo, pagamenti, API
Step 5: Inizia con OWASP Top 10 e tools automatici (nuclei, sqlmap)
Step 6: Testa manualmente la business logic (sconti, ruoli, workflow)
Step 7: Documenta OGNI cosa interessante
Step 8: Scrivi un report chiaro con PoC riproducibile in 5 minuti
Step 9: Submeti e rispondi velocemente a domande del triage
Step 10: Studia i report pubblici (HackerOne Hacktivity) per imparare
tips: 💡 Leggi almeno 50 report risolti su HackerOne Hacktivity prima di iniziare
💡 Concentrati su UN programma per almeno 2 settimane
💡 Le business logic bug pagano DI PIÙ delle XSS
💡 I bug race condition sono sottovalutati ma pagati
💡 Usa Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) per trovare endpoint dimenticati
💡 Controlla sempre le API mobile vs web
💡 Non riportare MAI self-XSS, clickjacking senza impatto
💡 Impara Burp a livello avanzato: macro, match/replace, scanner
💡 La qualità del report > quantità
💡 Network: Discord Bugcrowd, NahamSec, InsiderPhD, STÖK

descrizione: Improper Control of Filename for Include/Require Statement in PHP Program ('PHP Remote File Inclusion') vulnerability in Magepeople inc. WpTravelly tour-booking-manager allows PHP Local File Inclusion.This issue affects WpTravelly: from n/a through 2.3.8.

outOfScope: Attacchi DDoS / volumetrici
Social engineering su dipendenti
Test su ambienti di produzione con dati reali di utenti

Vulnerabilità in browser di terze parti (es. Chrome bugs)
Rate limiting issues senza impatto reale
Self-XSS (richiede azione della vittima)
Vulnerabilità che richiedono accesso fisico al device
Clickjacking su pagine senza azioni sensibili
Best practice senza impatto dimostrabile
Username/email enumeration su form pubblici
CSRF su endpoint non state-changing
Vulnerabilità già note pubblicamente senza PoC aggiuntivo

titolo: CVE-2026-122041: The Checkout Field Editor for WooCommerce (Pro) plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to unauthorized d...
descrizione: The Checkout Field Editor for WooCommerce (Pro) plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to unauthorized deletion of arbitrary attachments due to a missing capability/ownership check in the ajax_remove_uploaded() function in versions up to, and including, 3.8.0. The handler is registered for both wp_ajax and wp_ajax_nopriv and is gated solely by the 'file_handling_nonce' nonce, which is emitted inside the public checkout page markup (data-nonce attribute) whenever a File Upload checkout field is configured. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to delete arbitrary attachments (including those belonging to other users or posts) by submitting a crafted attachment_id, which can lead to loss of important media and potential denial of service.

descrizione: A flaw was found in the Keycloak server's client management component. When a client is created or imported with authorization services enabled, the system fails to properly clear an internal session attribute used during the setup process. This allows an authenticated attacker with client management permissions to bypass security controls and upload a malicious JavaScript policy, which is then executed on the server when an authorization request is made. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to run arbitrary code on the server, potentially compromising the entire system.

titolo:
CVE-2026-99271: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: line6: Clear prev_fbuf on...
descrizione:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ALSA: line6: Clear prev_fbuf on capture buffer release

A KASAN slab-use-after-free read was reported in submit_audio_out_urb()
when generating an impulse test signal:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in create_impulse_test_signal sound/usb/line6/playback.c:76 [inline]
  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in submit_audio_out_urb+0x1848/0x1b20 sound/usb/line6/playback.c:249
  Read of size 2 at addr ffff888008d74870 by task syz.2.3214/7785

  Allocated by task 11:
   kmem_cache_alloc_noprof+0x2f0/0x390 mm/slub.c:4144
   line6_buffer_acquire+0x1a1/0x220 sound/usb/line6/pcm.c:158
   line6_pcm_acquire+0xb6/0x230 sound/usb/line6/pcm.c:329
   line6_startup_work+0x3c/0x50 sound/usb/line6/driver.c:728

  Freed by task 7785:
   kfree+0xf8/0x390 mm/slub.c:6566
   line6_buffer_release sound/usb/line6/pcm.c:176 [inline]
   line6_buffer_release+0xa5/0xf0 sound/usb/line6/pcm.c:170
   __line6_pcm_release sound/usb/line6/pcm.c:305 [inline]
   line6_pcm_release+0x5a/0x80 sound/usb/line6/pcm.c:313
   snd_toneport_monitor_put+0x11b/0x190 sound/usb/line6/toneport.c:183

line6pcm->prev_fbuf points into the capture PCM stream buffer
(line6pcm->in.buffer), which is updated during audio_in_callback() to
feed rate synchronization, software monitoring, and impulse test signal
generation on playback side.

When all capture streams are closed, line6_buffer_release() frees
pstr->buffer with kfree().  However, it does not clear line6pcm->prev_fbuf.
If playback is subsequently started (e.g. via impulse test signal
volume control snd_line6_impulse_volume_put()), submit_audio_out_urb()
dereferences the stale pointer line6pcm->prev_fbuf under in.lock,
resulting in a slab-use-after-free read.

Clear prev_fbuf and prev_fsize in line6_buffer_release() when releasing
the capture stream buffer under in.lock, ensuring that no stale buffer
pointer can be accessed by submit_audio_out_urb().

titolo:
CVE-2026-99272: In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: validate the data ...
descrizione:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb: client: validate the data area in SMB2_read()

SMB2_read() copies le32_to_cpu(rsp->DataLength) bytes from
(char *)rsp + rsp->DataOffset without checking that the range lies
within the response actually received. A READ response with
DataOffset == 0 makes smb2_get_data_area_len() zero the data length, so
smb2_check_message() accepts a frame as short as the fixed response,
while SMB2_read() still uses the server-supplied DataLength, capped only
by CIFS_MAX_MSGSIZE and the caller's length.

A malicious server can answer the synchronous read used by the
mfsymlinks (or SFU) symlink parser with an 81-byte READ response
carrying DataOffset 0 and DataLength 1067, making the client copy 1067
bytes from a 448-byte receive object (KASAN slab-out-of-bounds; up to
16 KiB in the general case).

Clamp a zero (or header-overlapping) DataOffset to read_rsp_size, as
handle_read_data() does for the asynchronous path, and reject the
response unless DataOffset + DataLength fits within rsp_iov.iov_len.
The SMB1 helper was fixed the same way in 5be5bdda5863.

titolo: GHSA-89p3-fcch-88ph: NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in CCG lexicon parser (fromstring) on wide bracket bodies and operator chains
descrizione:
## Summary

The public CCG lexicon parser `nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring` parses caller-influenced lexicon text with two pure-Python loops whose cost is quadratic in the input width. A service that parses an untrusted CCG lexicon string can be driven into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU by a few-megabyte input, starving the request worker. No authentication or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

`matchBrackets` consumes a bracket body one character at a time with `inside = inside + rest[0]; rest = rest[1:]`. The `rest = rest[1:]` tail re-slice copies the entire remaining string on every iteration, so a flat bracket body costs O(n^2). `augParseCategory` drives a `while rest != "":` operator loop that re-copies the regular-expression match tail (`rest = app[3]`) once per operator, which is also O(n^2) over a long operator chain. The parser carries a recursion-depth guard (`MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 500`) that raises on deeply nested categories, but both quadratic loops run on flat input whose nesting depth stays at zero, so that guard never fires. No bound is applied to line length or category width before the text reaches these loops.

```text
Affected functions:
- nltk.ccg.lexicon.matchBrackets       (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:149-172; tail re-slice at line 168)
- nltk.ccg.lexicon.augParseCategory    (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:223-268; APP_RE tail re-copy at line 250)
Public entry point: nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:271), also re-exported as nltk.ccg.chart.fromstring.
```

## Impact

An attacker who can influence the CCG lexicon string parsed by an application causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The vulnerable path is network-reachable (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). Because the cost grows quadratically with attacker-chosen input size, a few-megabyte payload costs tens of seconds per core, and a small number of concurrent requests can exhaust worker threads. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The NLTK regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps regex matching only; it does not wrap these pure-Python slicing loops, so it provides no protection here.

## Proof of Concept

```text
Environment: nltk 3.10.3, regex 2026.9.10, CPython. Run the parser on the shipped public API.
```

```python
import nltk.ccg.lexicon as L

# Vector A: flat bracket body -> matchBrackets tail re-slice is O(n^2)
n = 400000
lex_a = ":- S\nw => (" + "a" * n + ")\n"

# Vector B: long operator chain -> augParseCategory tail re-copy is O(n^2)
m = 32000
lex_b = ":- a\nw => " + "a" + "/a" * m + "\n"

import time
for name, s in (("A", lex_a), ("B", lex_b)):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        L.fromstring(s)
    except Exception:
        pass  # downstream parse error is irrelevant; the CPU is already burned
    print(name, round(time.perf_counter() - t, 3), "s")
```

```text
Negative control (":- a\nw => (a/a)"):   ~0.00007 s
Vector A (matchBrackets, flat body):     n=50k 0.078s | 100k 0.260s | 200k 1.046s | 400k 2.083s   (~4x per doubling => O(n^2))
Vector B (augParseCategory, operators):  m=4k 0.078s | 8k 0.215s | 16k 0.485s | 32k 1.329s        (super-linear)
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** An application calls the public `nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring(lex_str)` (also reachable as `nltk.ccg.chart.fromstring`) on lexicon text the attacker can influence.
2. **Control:** The attacker fully controls the body width (a run of characters inside one bracket) and the operator-chain length; neither is capped by `fromstring`.
3. **Path:** `fromstring` splits input into lines and routes each category through `nextCategory`, which dispatches to `matchBrackets` (Vector A) or into the `augParseCategory` operator loop (Vector B).
4. **Guard:** The only relevant guard is the `MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 500` recursion-depth check. On flat input the recursion depth is zero, so `if _depth > max_depth` is never reached; the width loops run unbounded.
5. **Primitive:** The tail re-slice `rest = rest[1:]` and tail re-copy `rest = app[3]` execute a quadratic number of string copies.
6. **Result:** Sustained single-core CPU exhaustion; a few-megabyte lexicon costs tens of seconds and scales quadratically, blocking the parsing thread.

## Bypass Evidence

The one protection present on this path is the recursion-depth guard `MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 500` (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:22), checked at lexicon.py:153 and lexicon.py:228. It defends only against nesting depth and raises a bounded `ValueError` for deeply nested categories. The quadratic payloads here are flat: a single bracket body or a single operator run has nesting depth zero to one, so the depth check provably never fires while the width loops consume quadratic time. This was confirmed by running the shipped parser: the payloads complete without a `ValueError` or a regex `TimeoutError` while consuming quadratic CPU (Vector A shows a clean 4x cost per input doubling). A repository search finds no line-length or category-width cap anywhere on the `fromstring` path; the regex source-length limit bounds regex patterns, not lexicon text. The strongest disproof attempt (that CPython in-place string concatenation makes Vector A linear) fails because `rest = rest[1:]` is an unconditional copy of the remaining input that the concatenation fast path cannot elide, and the measured 4x-per-doubling ratio confirms the quadratic empirically.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: PyPI (pip)`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI, https://pypi.org/pypi/nltk/json)`
- `Fix status: 3.10.4`

The width-slicing loops ship in every release carrying the CCG lexicon parser and are present in the current latest published release, 3.10.3. The lower boundary was not bisected, so the introducing version is left open; the behavior long predates the recent regular-expression and recursion-depth hardening.

## Suggested Fix

Scan the bracket body and the operator chain with an index cursor into the original string (or a `collections.deque`) instead of repeatedly re-slicing or re-copying the tail, so each character is handled in constant amortized time. As defense in depth, impose an explicit bound on lexicon line length and category width at the `fromstring` chokepoint and raise a bounded error when it is exceeded, mirroring the existing depth guard. No configuration-only mitigation fully removes the exposure for a service that must parse untrusted lexicons; until a fix ships, callers should cap the size of accepted lexicon input and parse it under a CPU or time budget in an isolated worker.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).


## Fix status

PR: #3753 "[Do not merge yet] Fix GHSA-8mgp-746c-j5xp: URL-scheme bypass of pathsec.validate_path", open; head da55cab0e at the time of this note (a develop merge on top of 238f81500, the head on which the verdicts below were measured).

Fix commit: cf12a5e6a (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py: matchBrackets, nextCategory and augParseCategory thread a cursor instead of re-slicing the tail; the trailing capture group is dropped; MAX_PARSE_LEN=100000 caps the input).

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_89p3_fcch_88ph.py (on the PR). Verdict on the PR head: FIXED (scaling 4.4x over a 4x input; an over-cap chain is rejected by MAX_PARSE_LEN). The advisory PoC re-run on develop 2fa3f48fe: vector A (bracket body, 100k vs 400k) 15.8x and vector B (operator chain, 8k vs 32k) 11.3x over a 4x input, so develop is still VULNERABLE.

titolo: GHSA-r53h-rw34-8h97: NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in Tree.chomsky_normal_form right-factor binarization via list.pop(0)
descrizione:
## Summary

`Tree.chomsky_normal_form()` binarizes a parse tree and defaults to right factoring. For a node with N children the right-factor branch repeatedly removes the first element of a working list with `list.pop(0)`, which shifts all remaining elements each time, so binarizing one wide node costs O(N^2). An application that converts an attacker-supplied treebank tree to Chomsky Normal Form can be forced into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU by one wide flat tree. No authentication or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

In the default right-factor branch the transform executes `curNode[0:] = [nodeCopy.pop(0), newNode]` inside a loop over the N children of a node. `list.pop(0)` is O(len) because it shifts every remaining element down by one; performed N-2 times over a shrinking length-N list this sums to O(N^2). The left-factor branch instead uses `nodeCopy.pop()` (removing the last element), which is O(1) and linear overall, so the two branches differ only by this front-versus-back removal. No cap is placed on the child count of a node, and the public `Tree.fromstring` parser accepts an arbitrarily wide bracketed tree.

```text
Affected function:
- nltk.tree.transforms.chomsky_normal_form (nltk/tree/transforms.py; right-factor sink at line 168, O(1) left control at line 179)
Public entry points: nltk.tree.Tree.chomsky_normal_form (nltk/tree/tree.py:455, default factor="right"); nltk.tree.Tree.fromstring (nltk/tree/tree.py:592).
```

## Impact

An attacker who can influence the tree that an application normalizes to Chomsky Normal Form causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The path is network-reachable (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). Because the cost grows quadratically with the attacker-chosen child count, roughly 1.5 MB of treebank input costs about 14 seconds on one core and scales as N^2 above that. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The NLTK regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps regex matching only and does not wrap this pure-Python list loop.

## Proof of Concept

```text
Environment: nltk 3.10.3, CPython. Drive the public transform on a wide flat tree.
```

```python
import time
from nltk.tree import Tree

for N in (80000, 160000, 320000):
    s = "(S " + "(A a)" * N + ")"
    t = Tree.fromstring(s)
    start = time.perf_counter()
    t.chomsky_normal_form()          # default factor="right"
    print("right", N, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3), "s")
```

```text
right (default):  N=80000 1.972s | N=160000 5.004s (2.54x) | N=320000 14.518s (2.90x)   -> super-linear
left  (control):  N=80000 1.399s | N=160000 2.731s (1.95x) | N=320000  5.379s (1.97x)   -> linear
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** An application parses an attacker-influenced treebank string with the public `Tree.fromstring` and normalizes it with `Tree.chomsky_normal_form()`.
2. **Control:** The attacker controls the number of children of a node (a wide flat tree such as `(S (A a)(A a)...(A a))`); no child-count cap exists in `fromstring` or the transform.
3. **Path:** `Tree.chomsky_normal_form` delegates to `nltk.tree.transforms.chomsky_normal_form` with the default `factor="right"`.
4. **Guard:** None. There is no width bound on the loop, and the regex match timeout does not wrap this pure-Python list operation.
5. **Primitive:** `curNode[0:] = [nodeCopy.pop(0), newNode]` performs an O(N) front shift on each of N iterations.
6. **Result:** O(N^2) single-core CPU exhaustion; roughly 1.5 MB of input costs about 14 seconds and scales quadratically, blocking the processing thread.

## Bypass Evidence

There is no guard to bypass on this path: neither `Tree.fromstring` nor `chomsky_normal_form` caps the child count, and the regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps only regex matching, not this list loop. The finding was confirmed by fresh timing that isolates the cause: the right-factor default and the left-factor branch build the identical bounded head strings and copy the node once, so the only differing term is `pop(0)` versus `pop()`. The measured right-versus-left divergence grows with N (right rises toward a 4x per-doubling ratio while left holds near 2x), which proves a quadratic component beyond the shared linear costs. A relevant corroboration is that the inverse transform `un_chomsky_normal_form` was already rewritten to a single linear pass to remove exactly this quadratic class (see the comment at nltk/tree/transforms.py:195-201), while the forward default path retained the `pop(0)` idiom. The strongest disproof attempt (that the head-string join dominates and is linear) fails because that join is bounded and present in both branches and therefore cannot explain the branch-dependent quadratic growth.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: PyPI (pip)`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI, https://pypi.org/pypi/nltk/json)`
- `Fix status: 3.10.4`

The right-factor `pop(0)` idiom ships in every release carrying this transform and is present in the current latest published release, 3.10.3. The lower boundary was not bisected, so the introducing version is left open.

## Suggested Fix

Rewrite the right-factor binarization to avoid removing from the front of a list: iterate the children with an index cursor or a `collections.deque` so each step is constant time, mirroring the linear rebuild already applied to `un_chomsky_normal_form`. As defense in depth, bound the child count accepted for normalization and raise a clear error past a configurable maximum. No configuration-only mitigation removes the exposure for a service that normalizes untrusted trees; until a fix ships, callers should cap accepted tree width and run the transform under a CPU or time budget in an isolated worker.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).


## Fix status (2026-09-28)

PR: #3909 "Fix quadratic DoS in Tree.chomsky_normal_form right-factor binarization (GHSA-r53h-rw34-8h97)", merged 2026-09-23, merge commit 2f53e20ce on develop.

Fix commits: 457ebe349 (linear front consume in chomsky_normal_form) and 677857dca (refuse a binarisation that would nest a tree beyond MAX_TREE_DEPTH). Follow-up #3917 (merge 9ba132e43, commit f0686dea6) walks Tree equality and conversion with an explicit stack so the deep-tree tests pass on Python 3.10 and 3.11.

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_r53h_rw34_8h97.py; verdict on develop 2fa3f48fe: FIXED (chomsky_normal_form scales 5.1x over a 4x input).

titolo: GHSA-v8f3-6phw-6mh9: NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in ConllCorpusReader SRL instance builder via nested span rescan
descrizione:
## Summary

`ConllCorpusReader.srl_instances()` builds semantic-role-labeling instances from a CoNLL corpus block. For a sentence block with P predicates and P span columns, the instance builder rescans every span column (and every span within it) once per predicate while searching for each predicate's head, giving O(P^2 * R) work. A single well-formed block that places the head span in the last column forces the full scan on every predicate, so an application that reads an attacker-supplied CoNLL SRL corpus can be driven into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU. No authentication or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

`_get_srl_instances` iterates over the P predicates of a block; for each predicate it scans every span list and every span within it, using an inner `break` that stops only when a span tagged `V` or `C-V` containing the predicate word is found. When the sole head span is placed in the last span column, no earlier column matches, so the `for ... else: continue` construct traverses every span of every earlier column before matching. Over P predicates each scanning up to P columns of R spans, the cost is O(P^2 * R). The block is read whole with no size cap, and the grid-consistency check enforces only uniform column count, not a bound on P, R, or total work.

```text
Affected function:
- nltk.corpus.reader.conll.ConllCorpusReader._get_srl_instances (nltk/corpus/reader/conll.py:394-424; nested rescan at lines 405-419)
Public entry point: nltk.corpus.reader.conll.ConllCorpusReader.srl_instances (nltk/corpus/reader/conll.py:158-169).
```

## Impact

An attacker who can supply a CoNLL corpus that an application loads and iterates with `srl_instances()` causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The path is network-reachable through any corpus-ingestion surface (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). Because the cost is super-linear in attacker-chosen predicate and column counts, a roughly 1 MB crafted corpus pins a core for tens of seconds and a few megabytes reaches minutes. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The NLTK regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps regex matching only and does not cover this pure-Python nested loop over the parsed grid. Exploitation requires the application to use the SRL-specific API on untrusted CoNLL data with `words`, `pos`, `tree`, and `srl` columns; a deployment that never calls `srl_instances()` is unaffected.

## Proof of Concept

```text
Environment: nltk 3.10.3, CPython. Stage a crafted CoNLL corpus under an authorized data root and iterate srl_instances().
Corpus construction: one blank-line-delimited block with P predicate rows and P SRL span columns, the sole "V" head span in the last column.
```

```python
import time, os, tempfile
from nltk.corpus.reader.conll import ConllCorpusReader

def build_block(n):
    # n predicates, n SRL columns; the single V head placed in the last column
    # (columns: words pos tree srl...): emit n predicate rows and n SRL span
    # columns, with the single "V" head span placed in the final column.
    ...

for n in (40, 80, 160, 320):
    root = tempfile.mkdtemp()
    open(os.path.join(root, "c.conll"), "w").write(build_block(n))
    r = ConllCorpusReader(root, ["c.conll"], ("words", "pos", "tree", "srl"))
    t = time.perf_counter()
    list(r.srl_instances())
    print(n, round(time.perf_counter() - t, 3), "s")
```

```text
Negative control (single predicate): n=40 -> 1.88 ms ; n=320 -> 4.45 ms      (flat)
Attack (P=R=n):  n=40 -> 0.022s (10 KB) | n=80 -> 0.148s (39 KB) | n=160 -> 1.164s (156 KB) | n=320 -> 10.002s (619 KB)
```

The attack timing rises about 8x per doubling of n while the file grows only about 4x, confirming super-linear cost driven by attacker-chosen predicate and column count; the single-predicate control stays in the millisecond range.

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** An application loads an attacker-supplied CoNLL corpus (columns include `srl`) and iterates it with the public `ConllCorpusReader(...).srl_instances()`.
2. **Control:** The attacker controls the predicate count P, the span-column count, and the placement of the single head span; the block is read whole with no size cap.
3. **Path:** `srl_instances()` calls `_get_srl_instances`, which pairs each predicate against the span columns via a doubly-nested scan.
4. **Guard:** The inner `break` on the first matching `V` or `C-V` head is defeated by placing the sole head span in the last column, so every earlier column is scanned in full. The path-containment sandbox bounds where files load, not how much work a block costs.
5. **Primitive:** The nested rescan performs O(P^2 * R) span comparisons with no work cap or timeout.
6. **Result:** Sustained single-core CPU exhaustion; a roughly 1 MB corpus costs tens of seconds and scales super-linearly, blocking the processing thread.

## Bypass Evidence

The only short-circuit on this path is the inner `break` that fires when a predicate's `V` or `C-V` head span is found. It is defeated by construction: placing the sole head span in the last span column means no earlier column matches, so the `for ... else: continue` traverses every span of every earlier column for every predicate. This was confirmed in source (nltk/corpus/reader/conll.py:405-419) and reproduced end-to-end through the real public `srl_instances()` API, where the attack timing scales super-linearly while a single-predicate control stays flat. The path-containment sandbox is a file-location control and imposes no bound on parse cost, and the regular-expression timeout does not wrap this loop. The strongest disproof attempts (that Python `range` membership is O(1) so the loop is linear, and that the `break` fires early) both fail: the O(1) membership test is evaluated once per span, and the number of spans traversed is exactly what the last-column head placement maximizes.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: PyPI (pip)`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI, https://pypi.org/pypi/nltk/json)`
- `Fix status: 3.10.4`

The nested rescan ships in every release carrying this reader and is present in the current latest published release, 3.10.3. The lower boundary was not bisected, so the introducing version is left open; the behavior predates the recent regular-expression hardening.

## Suggested Fix

Replace the per-predicate linear search over all span columns with a single pass that indexes head spans by word position (for example, build a map from word index to the owning span column once, then look up each predicate in constant time), reducing the total cost to about O(P * R). As defense in depth, bound the predicate and span counts accepted from a single block and process untrusted corpora under a CPU or time budget. No configuration-only mitigation removes the exposure for a service that must read untrusted CoNLL SRL data; until a fix ships, callers should cap accepted corpus size and isolate the parsing worker.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).


## Fix status (2026-09-28)

PR: #3753 "[Do not merge yet] Fix GHSA-8mgp-746c-j5xp: URL-scheme bypass of pathsec.validate_path", open; head da55cab0e at the time of this note (a develop merge on top of 238f81500, the head on which the verdicts below were measured).

Fix commit: cf12a5e6a "Patch seven algorithmic-DoS and path/exec GHSA classes across all affected modules" (ConllCorpusReader._get_srl_instances builds a one-pass wordnum to spanlist index instead of rescanning per predicate).

Probe: nltk/test/unit/security_probes/ghsa_v8f3_6phw_6mh9.py (on the PR). Verdict on the PR head: FIXED (srl_instances scaled 3.9x over 4x predicates). The same probe run against develop 2fa3f48fe: VULNERABLE (45.8x over 4x predicates).

titolo: GHSA-fg9w-wfp5-j933: NLTK: BllipParser passes caller-supplied model paths to the bllipparser C extension with no pathsec check, enabling arbitrary read
descrizione:
## Summary

`BllipParser` in `nltk/parse/bllip.py` hands caller-supplied filesystem paths to the native `bllipparser` C extension without routing them through NLTK's `pathsec` validation. The constructor parameters `parser_model`, `reranker_features`, and `reranker_weights`, and the alternative `from_unified_model_dir()` entry point, flow directly to the C extension's `load_parser_model()` and `load_reranker_model()` calls, which open and read the given path at the OS level. Any application that passes an attacker-influenced path to this API reads a file of the attacker's choosing from anywhere on the filesystem, outside the NLTK data roots that every other NLTK tool wrapper confines access to.

## Root Cause

As of NLTK 3.10.0, `SECURITY.md` documents a centralized I/O security module (`nltk.pathsec`) with strict enforcement enabled by default, under which file-backed resources must resolve inside allowed NLTK data directories. For paths handed to external tools and native extensions that open files themselves, the module provides `validate_tool_path()`, which runs name-safety checks, rejects option-shaped, URL-shaped, and traversal inputs, opens the path with `O_NOFOLLOW` requiring a regular single-linked file, and returns the validated string the caller must use. Every sibling tool wrapper applies it. `BllipParser` applies none of it: the module imports only `ParserI`, `safe_print`, and `Tree`, with zero `pathsec` references, so the three model-path parameters reach the C extension unchecked. The violated invariant is that NLTK tool wrappers must bound caller-supplied native-tool paths to the data roots before the native code opens them.

```text
nltk/parse/bllip.py:125-131   BllipParser.__init__ accepts parser_model,
                              reranker_features, reranker_weights (no validation)
nltk/parse/bllip.py:164       self.rrp.load_parser_model(parser_model, ...)   -> C extension open
nltk/parse/bllip.py:166-170   self.rrp.load_reranker_model(features_filename=...,
                              weights_filename=...)                          -> C extension open
nltk/parse/bllip.py:218-255   from_unified_model_dir(model_dir) -> __init__ (no validation)
nltk/parse/bllip.py:9-11      imports: ParserI, safe_print, Tree (no pathsec import)
```

## Impact

An application that uses `BllipParser` (requiring the optional `bllipparser` package to be installed) and that passes a model path derived from untrusted input to the constructor or to `from_unified_model_dir()` allows that input to designate an arbitrary filesystem path. The native extension opens and reads the designated file into process memory to parse it as model data. This defeats the pathsec data-root confinement that NLTK applies to all other native-tool model loads. The attacker-controlled path can target files outside the NLTK data directories, for example local configuration or credential files readable by the process. Content disclosure to the attacker depends on how the application surfaces parser errors or results; file existence, size, and open behavior provide an oracle regardless. Because the same unvalidated path also skips the checks that refuse a non-regular file or an over-large model, the attacker can instead designate a FIFO, socket, device, or directory, or an oversized regular file, so the native load blocks or reads unbounded data into memory and the component performing the parse suffers reduced performance or a stalled worker. The primitive demonstrated by source analysis is attacker control of which file the process opens and reads.

## Proof of Concept

```text
Requires the optional bllipparser C extension to be installed
(pip install bllipparser) so that RerankingParser.load_parser_model
is available. No NLTK data download is needed to exercise the path.
```

```python
# An application forwards an untrusted "model" path into BllipParser.
from nltk.parse.bllip import BllipParser

# Attacker-controlled value reaches the constructor unchanged.
untrusted_path = "/etc/passwd"
BllipParser(parser_model=untrusted_path)
# The bllipparser C extension opens and reads untrusted_path at the OS
# level with no NLTK pathsec confinement to the data roots.
```

```text
Structural confirmation without the optional extension installed:

$ grep -n "pathsec\|validate_path\|validate_tool" nltk/parse/bllip.py
(no output)

$ grep -n "validate_tool_path" nltk/tag/crf.py nltk/tag/hunpos.py \
      nltk/tag/stanford.py nltk/parse/malt.py
nltk/tag/crf.py:140
nltk/tag/crf.py:311
nltk/tag/hunpos.py:111
nltk/tag/stanford.py:85
nltk/tag/stanford.py:137
nltk/parse/malt.py:340
nltk/parse/malt.py:344

BllipParser is the only native-tool wrapper with no validate_tool_path call.
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** An application imports `BllipParser` (exported at `nltk/parse/bllip.py:83` and re-exported at `nltk/parse/__init__.py:47`) and constructs it with a model path influenced by untrusted input.
2. **Control:** The attacker controls the `parser_model`, `reranker_features`, or `reranker_weights` string (or the `model_dir` passed to `from_unified_model_dir()` at `nltk/parse/bllip.py:218`); it is accepted as an arbitrary string with no type or content constraint.
3. **Path:** The value flows unchanged from `BllipParser.__init__` (`nltk/parse/bllip.py:125`) to `self.rrp.load_parser_model(parser_model, ...)` at `nltk/parse/bllip.py:164`, and the reranker values to `self.rrp.load_reranker_model(...)` at `nltk/parse/bllip.py:166-170`.
4. **Guard:** No pathsec guard is present on this path. `nltk/parse/bllip.py` imports no pathsec symbol, so `validate_tool_path()` (the guard applied by every sibling wrapper) is never invoked before the native open.
5. **Primitive:** The `bllipparser` C extension performs an OS-level open and read of the supplied path to parse model data, reaching the filesystem directly.
6. **Result:** A file at an attacker-chosen path, including locations outside the NLTK data roots, is opened and read by the process, bypassing the pathsec data-root confinement enforced elsewhere.

## Bypass Evidence

The relevant protection is `nltk.pathsec.validate_tool_path()` (`nltk/pathsec.py:950`), documented as bounding "a filesystem path handed to an external tool to read or write" and designed exactly for native loaders that open the file themselves. The strongest counter-argument is that `SECURITY.md` disclaims being "a general operating-system sandbox" and does "not prevent all unsafe behavior an application might perform outside NLTK." That disclaimer concerns application code outside NLTK, not NLTK's own tool wrappers: the project added `validate_tool_path()` and applied it to `CRFTagger.set_model_file()` (`nltk/tag/crf.py:140`), `HunposTagger` (`nltk/tag/hunpos.py:111`), `StanfordTagger` (`nltk/tag/stanford.py:85,137`), and `MaltParser` (`nltk/parse/malt.py:340,344`), with the CRFTagger and HunposTagger wrappers citing a prior tool-path advisory and explaining that `pathsec.open` cannot be used because the C extension does its own open. `BllipParser` is the single native-tool wrapper that omits the guard. The alternative `from_unified_model_dir()` path offers no mitigation: `get_unified_model_parameters()` belongs to the third-party `bllipparser` package and performs no NLTK data-root validation, so the derived sub-paths reach the constructor and the C extension unchecked.

## Affected Versions

- **Ecosystem:** `pip`
- **Package:** `nltk`
- **Confirmed affected range:** `>= 3.10.0, <= 3.10.3`
- **Latest release checked:** `3.10.3` ([PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/nltk/3.10.3/))
- **Fix status:** 3.10.4

The lower bound is 3.10.0 because the pathsec enforcement model and the `validate_tool_path()` guard were introduced in that release; before 3.10.0 no such boundary existed for NLTK to violate. The missing validation persists unchanged through 3.10.3, the current PyPI release, and on the repository default branch (no `pathsec`, `validate_path`, or `validate_tool` reference exists in `nltk/parse/bllip.py`). No fixed release is established.

## Suggested Fix

Validate every caller-supplied native-tool path in `BllipParser` before it reaches the `bllipparser` C extension, matching the pattern already used by the other wrappers. In `BllipParser.__init__`, pass `parser_model`, `reranker_features`, and `reranker_weights` through `nltk.pathsec.validate_tool_path()` (with `max_bytes=MAX_TOOL_MODEL_BYTES` and `require_private=True`, as `CRFTagger.set_model_file()` does) and build the C-extension arguments from the returned strings so a path swapped after the check is not reopened. Because `parser_model` denotes a model directory for this loader, the fix must cover the directory argument and the reranker file arguments, and should apply equally to the paths derived inside `from_unified_model_dir()`. As an interim measure, applications should refuse to pass untrusted input as any `BllipParser` model path and should load models only through `nltk.data.find()`, which already enforces pathsec confinement.

---

Reported by zx.

titolo: GHSA-qfx6-q44v-9qqw: ag-psd can exhaust memory when parsing crafted PSD dimensions
descrizione:
### Summary
readPsd() commits the image/layer buffers from the declared header geometry (width x height x channels x depth, and per-layer rectangles) before validating those values against the actual data. A tiny crafted PSD declaring huge geometry forces a multi-gigabyte allocation.

### Impact
On ag-psd 30.2.0, Node 24, a 52-byte PSD makes readPsd(buf) commit ~3.17 GB (measured peak RSS) in ~0.45 s before throwing a catchable RangeError ("Offset is outside the bounds of the DataView") — about 61,000,000x amplification. Because the buffer is committed before validation, the allocation OOM-kills the process before the error on essentially any host (uncatchable), and concurrent requests exhaust memory. Any service reading untrusted PSDs with ag-psd is exposed to a remote DoS.

This is distinct from #39 and #206, which involve genuinely large PSDs (memory proportional to real data). Here the input is 52 bytes: the file declares enormous geometry that is never present, so the allocation is driven by an unvalidated header field, not by actual content, an uncontrolled-allocation denial-of-service vulnerability, not proportional memory use.

### Steps to reproduce
The PoC is a 52-byte PSD (sha256 a1146a6fabdfef289472f99a56851249e7a46e8d19d4d8bf85fe833e2f0158b6). Reconstruct with:

    base64 -d > poc.psd <<'EOF'
    OEJQUwABAAAAAAAAAA0AADcuAAA58wAgAAMAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAdEgNZv+i9bc9ygd2A==
    EOF

Then (commits ~3.17 GB before throwing a catchable RangeError):

    const { readPsd } = require('ag-psd');
    const buf = require('fs').readFileSync('poc.psd');
    readPsd(buf.buffer.slice(buf.byteOffset, buf.byteOffset + buf.byteLength));

### Root cause
psdReader.js sizes the off-heap typed-array buffers from the declared header dimensions (and per-layer rectangles, a second independent lever) before validating against the available bytes.

### Suggested fix
Validate the declared dimensions, channel count, depth, and per-layer rectangles against the actual input length (and a sane maximum) before allocating.

titolo: GHSA-pp88-jhwj-5qh5: File Browser: Trailing-slash directory deletion leaves public shares active for recreated paths
descrizione:
## Summary

File Browser v2.63.15 can leave a public directory share behind when the shared directory is deleted through a path with a trailing slash. The share cleanup path calls `DeleteWithPathPrefix(file.Path, userID)`, but the Bolt backend performs the database prefix query with the unnormalized argument before trimming the slash for boundary checks. For a stored share at `/a`, deleting `/a/` queries for paths prefixed by `/a/`, so the exact `/a` share is never loaded and never deleted.

If a directory with the same path is later recreated, the stale public share becomes active again and exposes the new directory contents through the old public URL.

## Impact

An authenticated user with share, download, and delete permissions can create a valid public share, delete the shared path with a trailing slash, and leave the public link in storage. The link is dormant while the path does not exist, but it exposes future content if the same path is recreated later. The final data exposure is unauthenticated through the public share URL.

This bypasses the intended lifecycle cleanup around public shares and is adjacent to the recent public-share path-existence and prefix-boundary fixes.

## Reproduction

The following test was run against v2.63.15, commit `be23ab3a15bf957928ecfed88de5ab67850c1b9c`.

1. Create a scoped user with share, download, and delete permissions.
2. Create `/a/old.txt` in that user's scope.
3. Store a valid public share row with `Hash: "h"`, `UserID: 1`, and `Path: "/a"`.
4. Send an authenticated delete request for `/a/` through the resource delete handler.
5. Confirm the directory is deleted.
6. Confirm share hash `h` still exists in storage.
7. Recreate `/a/future.txt`.
8. Request the public share handler at `h/` and observe that the unauthenticated response includes `future.txt`.

Command used for the local proof:

```bash
go test ./http -run TestValidationTrailingSlashDeleteLeavesExactDirectoryShare -count=1 -v
```

Observed result:

```text
=== RUN   TestValidationTrailingSlashDeleteLeavesExactDirectoryShare
--- PASS: TestValidationTrailingSlashDeleteLeavesExactDirectoryShare (0.03s)
PASS
ok  github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/http  0.044s
```

## Root cause

`storage/bolt/share.go` queries the share index before normalizing the path:

```go
func (s shareBackend) DeleteWithPathPrefix(pathPrefix string, userID uint) error {
    var links []share.Link
    if err := s.db.Prefix("Path", pathPrefix, &links); err != nil {
        ...
    }

    prefix := strings.TrimRight(pathPrefix, "/")

    for _, link := range links {
        if link.UserID != userID {
            continue
        }

        if link.Path != prefix && !strings.HasPrefix(link.Path, prefix+"/") {
            continue
        }
        ...
    }
}
```

For `pathPrefix == "/a/"`, the database prefix query can return descendants such as `/a/child`, but it does not return the exact share path `/a`. The later `TrimRight` cannot delete the exact share because that row was not loaded from storage.

`http/resource.go` passes the request-derived path into this cleanup before removing the resource:

```go
file, err := files.NewFileInfo(... Path: r.URL.Path ...)
...
err = d.store.Share.DeleteWithPathPrefix(file.Path, d.user.ID)
...
return d.user.Fs.RemoveAll(r.URL.Path)
```

A request for `/a/` therefore removes the directory but misses the exact `/a` share row.

## Remediation

Normalize the path before querying the share index, and cover both the exact normalized path and its descendants. Add regression tests where a stored share path `/a` is removed by `DeleteWithPathPrefix("/a/", userID)` and where `DELETE /api/resources/a/` deletes the exact public share row.

Fixed in version 2.63.17.

titolo: GHSA-gpwc-27cw-rh9r: NLTK: Quadratic CPU exhaustion in LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize via unguarded onset reversal loop
descrizione:
## Summary

`LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize` in the NLTK tokenizer package contains an unguarded O(n^2) processing loop. When the method is called on a single token that consists of a long run of vowels (for example `"a" * n`), it consumes CPU time proportional to the square of the token length. An attacker who can supply an untrusted token to this public tokenizer API can force a single request to saturate one CPU core for a prolonged period, degrading availability of any service that syllabifies attacker-controlled text. No authentication, special configuration, or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

The method walks the token in reverse and, on every iteration after the first vowel is seen, evaluates the membership test `char_lower + current_onset[::-1] in self.legal_onsets`. The set `legal_onsets` is built by `onset()`, which returns only the characters up to the first vowel, so every member is vowel-free. For an all-vowel token the first branch can therefore never match, `onset` never becomes `True`, and the reset branch that would clear `current_onset` is never reached. As a result `current_onset` grows by one character on every iteration. Building `current_onset[::-1]` and hashing the resulting string costs O(k) on iteration k, and this is repeated for k from 1 to n, giving total cost O(n^2). The security invariant that is violated is bounded per-token work: there is no length cap on this code path, so untrusted token length translates directly into quadratic CPU consumption.

```text
Affected function: LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize
Source: nltk/tokenize/legality_principle.py (membership-test sink at line 133; loop over token[::-1] beginning at line 126)
Helper establishing the vowel-free onset set: LegalitySyllableTokenizer.onset (nltk/tokenize/legality_principle.py, returns prefix up to first vowel)
```

## Impact

An attacker who controls a token passed to `LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize` can trigger quadratic CPU work. In the reviewed release a token of roughly 64,000 vowel characters takes about 1.8 seconds on a single core, and the cost grows with the square of the length, so a token in the hundreds of kilobytes to megabyte range consumes a core for many seconds to minutes. Memory use is linear. The demonstrated capability is single-core CPU exhaustion leading to denial of service or latency degradation in any network-reachable component that syllabifies untrusted input. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact; the effect is availability degradation of the affected process. The plausible operational consequence, where multiple concurrent requests are used, is exhaustion of the available worker pool; this is inferred from the per-request cost and was not itself executed against a live deployment.

## Proof of Concept

`Requires only the released nltk package; no corpus download is needed because the quadratic behavior is driven entirely by the attacker token, not by the size of the legal-onset set.`

1. Construct a tokenizer with any small onset source.
2. Call `tokenize` with an all-vowel token of increasing length and time each call.
3. Compare against a consonant-alternating control token of equal length.

```python
import time
from nltk.tokenize import LegalitySyllableTokenizer

tok = LegalitySyllableTokenizer("tr c d".split())  # tiny 3-word onset source
for n in (8000, 16000, 32000):
    payload = "a" * n
    start = time.perf_counter()
    tok.tokenize(payload)
    print("vowel-run", n, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3))

control = "ba" * 32000  # equal-length linear control
start = time.perf_counter()
tok.tokenize(control)
print("control", 64000, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3))
```

```text
vowel-run 8000 0.031
vowel-run 16000 0.120
vowel-run 32000 0.468   (about 4x per doubling => O(n^2))
control 64000 0.004     (linear, roughly 130x faster at larger size)
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** `LegalitySyllableTokenizer` is exported from `nltk.tokenize` and `tokenize` is a public, documented method reachable by any service that syllabifies untrusted text.
2. **Control:** The attacker fully controls the `token` argument, including its length and character content; a run of vowels such as `"a" * n` survives with no normalization or length reduction.
3. **Path:** The token flows into the reverse walk at `nltk/tokenize/legality_principle.py:126` and reaches the membership-test at line 133 on every iteration past the first vowel.
4. **Guard:** There is no length cap on this path. The sibling `SyllableTokenizer` received a `MAX_TOKEN_LEN` cap during the project hardening work, but `legality_principle.py` received no such guard.
5. **Primitive:** Repeated O(k) construction and hashing of `current_onset[::-1]` inside the loop yields cumulative O(n^2) CPU work.
6. **Result:** A single request with a large vowel-run token exhausts one CPU core for a sustained period, degrading service availability.

## Bypass Evidence

No guard blocks this path. Membership-set analysis shows the first branch at line 133 cannot fire for a vowel character because `legal_onsets` is provably vowel-free (it is derived from `onset()`, which stops at the first vowel), so `onset` never becomes `True` and `current_onset` is never reset. The strongest refutations were attempted and failed: (1) the hypothesis that the quadratic depends on a large or specific onset corpus was disproven by reproducing the same O(n^2) growth with a three-word onset source, showing the cost is driven solely by the attacker token; (2) the hypothesis that an upstream length cap neutralizes long tokens was disproven by direct source inspection, which found no `MAX_TOKEN_LEN` or equivalent clamp on this class and confirmed the default word-tokenization path does not call this class; (3) the hypothesis that this is covered by existing hardening was disproven, since the project quadratic-DoS test suite exercises the sibling `SyllableTokenizer` but contains no test for `LegalitySyllableTokenizer`, and no commit added a cap to this file. This is a fix-missed sibling of the accepted algorithmic-complexity class, not a previously remediated issue.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: pip`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: >= 3.6, <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI)`
- `Fix status: not fixed`

The vulnerable loop is present and unguarded in the current released artifact 3.10.3, verified by direct source inspection and by reproducing the quadratic curve. The lower bound of 3.6 reflects when the affected module first shipped; the disclosure-relevant fact is that the latest published release is affected and no fix has been released.

## Suggested Fix

Enforce a bound on per-token work in `LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize`, consistent with the `MAX_TOKEN_LEN` guard already applied to the sibling `SyllableTokenizer`. Options include rejecting or truncating tokens above a configurable maximum length before the reverse walk, or restructuring the onset accumulation so the loop does not repeatedly build and hash a growing reversed string (for example by maintaining the onset in its final orientation and comparing without an O(k) reversal each iteration). The remediation should cover any caller that passes untrusted tokens, not just the default word-tokenization path. As an interim mitigation, deployments that expose syllabification of untrusted input can cap request and token sizes at the application boundary to bound the worst-case token length.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

## Fix status (2026-09-28)

PR: #3895 "[WIP] Bound algorithmic-DoS and uncontrolled-recursion vectors (CWE-400/407/674/1333)", open, head b22ebe144.

Fix commit: e20c40e26 "Bound tokenizer/parser algorithmic DoS (ffr9/gpwc/8fx7)" (LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize refuses a token longer than MAX_TOKEN_LEN=4096 with ValueError naming CWE-407).

No probe. The advisory PoC re-run: on the PR head the 32k vowel token is refused and under the cap the tokenizer scales 0.8x over a 4x input (1k vs 4k); on develop 2fa3f48fe it scales 14.2x over a 4x input (8k 0.087 s, 32k 1.245 s), so develop is still VULNERABLE. The related merged PR #3911 (25beee962) bounds the SyllableTokenizer vowel accumulation, a different tokenizer, and does not cover this sink.

titolo: GHSA-ffr9-mgrr-wcvr: NLTK: Quadratic CPU exhaustion in TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize via list.pop(0) in quote-restore loop
descrizione:
## Summary

`TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize` in the NLTK tokenizer package contains an unguarded O(n^2) processing loop in its quote-restoration step. When the method is invoked on text containing a long run of double-quote characters (for example `'"' * n`), it performs a `list.pop(0)` operation once per quote token, and because `list.pop(0)` is O(length), the total cost grows with the square of the input length. An attacker who can supply untrusted text to this public span-tokenization API can force a single request to saturate one CPU core for a prolonged period, degrading availability. No authentication, special configuration, or user interaction is required.

## Root Cause

Inside `span_tokenize`, when the input contains double or repeated quotes, the code builds `matched`, a list with one entry per quote occurrence, and then reconstructs tokens in a comprehension that calls `matched.pop(0)` for each token that is a quote. Removing the first element of a Python list is an O(len(list)) operation because all remaining elements are shifted. For an all-quote input the tokenizer produces n quote tokens and `matched` has n entries, so `pop(0)` is called n times, each time on a list of shrinking but still linear length, giving cumulative O(n^2) CPU work. The violated invariant is bounded per-input work: there is no length cap on `span_tokenize` or the underlying `tokenize`, so untrusted input length translates into quadratic processing time. The neighboring `align_tokens` call is linear and is not the quadratic term.

```text
Affected function: TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize
Source: nltk/tokenize/treebank.py
  - branch selector at line 203
  - matched list built at line 205
  - quadratic sink matched.pop(0) at line 209
  - linear align_tokens call at line 215
```

## Impact

An attacker who controls text passed to `TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize` can trigger quadratic CPU work. In the reviewed release, an all-quote input of 128,000 characters takes about 1.76 seconds and 256,000 characters about 6.57 seconds on a single core, with cost growing as the square of the length. Memory use is linear. The demonstrated capability is single-core CPU exhaustion producing denial of service or latency degradation in any network-reachable component that uses span tokenization on untrusted input, such as offset, annotation, or highlighting pipelines. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact. The plausible operational consequence, where multiple concurrent requests are used, is worker-pool exhaustion; this is inferred from the measured per-request cost and was not executed against a live deployment.

## Proof of Concept

`Requires only the released nltk package; no corpus download is needed.`

1. Instantiate `TreebankWordTokenizer`.
2. Call `span_tokenize` on an all-double-quote string of increasing length and time each call.
3. Compare against an equal-token-count control input that avoids the quote branch.

```python
import time
from nltk.tokenize import TreebankWordTokenizer

tok = TreebankWordTokenizer()
for n in (32000, 64000, 128000, 256000):
    payload = '"' * n
    start = time.perf_counter()
    list(tok.span_tokenize(payload))
    print("quote-run", n, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3))

control = "a " * 128000  # comparable token count, avoids the pop(0) branch
start = time.perf_counter()
list(tok.span_tokenize(control))
print("control", round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3))
```

```text
quote-run 32000 0.23
quote-run 64000 0.52
quote-run 128000 1.76
quote-run 256000 6.57   (about 4x per doubling => O(n^2))
control 0.16            (roughly 11x faster, isolates pop(0))
```

## Attack Chain

1. **Exposure:** `TreebankWordTokenizer` is exported from `nltk.tokenize` and `span_tokenize` is a public, documented method reachable by any service that span-tokenizes untrusted text.
2. **Control:** The attacker fully controls the `text` argument; a run of double-quote characters such as `'"' * n` survives to the quote branch unchanged.
3. **Path:** The branch selector at line 203 (`'"' in text` or `"''" in text`) is satisfied by the payload, entering the vulnerable branch; `matched` is built at line 205 with n entries and the reconstruction comprehension runs at line 209.
4. **Guard:** There is no length cap on `span_tokenize` or `tokenize`. The regex timeout backstop in `nltk/redos.py` only wraps regular-expression operations and does not cover the pure-Python `list.pop(0)` sink; a 256,000-character input ran to completion in 6.57 seconds with no timeout raised.
5. **Primitive:** `matched.pop(0)` executed once per quote token, each call O(len(matched)), yields cumulative O(n^2) CPU work.
6. **Result:** A single request with a large quote-run input exhausts one CPU core for a sustained period, degrading service availability.

## Bypass Evidence

No guard blocks this path. Direct inspection found no `MAX_TOKEN_LEN` or length check in `nltk/tokenize/treebank.py`, in contrast to the sibling `sonority_sequencing.py` which does cap token length. The strongest refutations were attempted and failed: (1) the hypothesis that `tokenize` collapses repeated quotes so few `pop(0)` calls occur was disproven by observing that `tokenize('"' * n)` yields exactly n quote tokens and timing showing about 4x growth per doubling, while an equal-token-count non-quote control ran roughly 11x faster; (2) the hypothesis that the project regex-timeout backstop already caps this cost was disproven by running a 256,000-character input to normal completion in 6.57 seconds with no `TimeoutError`, confirming the backstop wraps only regex operations and not `list.pop(0)`; (3) the hypothesis that this line was already audited was disproven, since the project quadratic-DoS test suite explicitly clears the neighboring `align_tokens` line reached through `span_tokenize` but contains no test for the `pop(0)` loop, an audited-neighbor pattern where the adjacent line was checked and this one was missed. The seed remediation touched a different module and no advisory covers this sink.

## Affected Versions

- `Ecosystem: pip`
- `Package: nltk`
- `Confirmed affected range: >= 3.2.5, <= 3.10.3`
- `Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI)`
- `Fix status: not fixed`

The vulnerable `pop(0)` loop is present and unguarded in the current released artifact 3.10.3, verified by direct source inspection and by reproducing the quadratic curve through fresh execution. The lower bound of 3.2.5 reflects when the affected quote-restoration code shipped; the disclosure-relevant fact is that the latest published release is affected and no fix has been released.

## Suggested Fix

Replace the O(n) `list.pop(0)` pattern with an O(1) consumption strategy, for example iterating over `matched` with an index or an iterator, or using `collections.deque` with `popleft()`, so that the quote-restoration step runs in linear time overall. Additionally, consider enforcing a configurable maximum input length in `span_tokenize` consistent with the caps applied to sibling tokenizers, and ensure the fix covers all callers that pass untrusted text. As an interim mitigation, deployments that expose span tokenization of untrusted input can cap request and input sizes at the application boundary to bound the worst-case length.

Reported by zx (GitHub: @manus-pi).

## Fix status (2026-09-28)

PR: #3753 "[Do not merge yet] Fix GHSA-8mgp-746c-j5xp: URL-scheme bypass of pathsec.validate_path", open; head da55cab0e at the time of this note (a develop merge on top of 238f81500, the head on which the verdicts below were measured).
